title: The Astronaut's Diary
summary: A fictional astronaut's diary entries describe daily life on a space station, a small equipment problem she solves with a crewmate, and what she misses about home.
poll: Living on a space station for months would be more exciting than hard.

versions.title: A Diary from Space
versions.text:
Day 1.

I am an astronaut. I live on a space station. It flies high above Earth.

Up here, things float. I float, too! I do not walk. I pull myself with my hands.

I wake up and do exercise. I eat food from a bag. Then I look out at Earth. It looks like a blue ball.

I write in my diary. I want to share my trip.

Day 2.

Today, a light blinked red. It was on the air filter. The filter cleans our air.

I felt scared. My crewmate came to help. Dust had blocked the filter! We cleaned it well. The light turned green.

I was so glad. We fixed it fast.

Day 3.

I think of home today. I miss my mom and dad. I miss walking on the ground.

There is no pull here. We call that pull gravity. It holds things down on Earth.

I also miss my food. My food here comes in bags.

But space is grand. Our ship flies around Earth fast. I see the sun rise many times.

Soon I will go home. I will not forget this trip.

versions.title: The Astronaut's Diary
versions.text:
Day 1.

I am an astronaut, and I currently live aboard a space station that orbits high above Earth. It circles the planet roughly once every ninety minutes, at nearly twenty-eight thousand kilometers per hour. Keeping this diary helps me remember every detail of my mission. I write a new entry each day and send some down to mission control for students to read.

Up here, everything floats, including me. Instead of walking through the station, I pull myself from module to module using handles bolted to the walls. Loose tools or pens must be kept secured, or they drift away.

My daily routine always begins with about an hour of exercise. This helps keep my muscles and bones strong, even though there is almost no gravity pulling on them here. Then I eat breakfast from a sealed bag, since loose food would otherwise float away and drift into sensitive equipment nearby.

Day 2.

Today, a warning light suddenly blinked red on the air filter, the device that removes dust and keeps our air safe to breathe. At first, I felt genuinely worried. An unfixed filter problem can quickly become dangerous, and mission control would need to be told immediately if we could not solve it ourselves.

My crewmate hurried over from another module to help me investigate. Together, we discovered that fine dust had slowly clogged the filter's screen over several weeks of regular use. Carefully, we removed it, cleaned every part by hand, and reinstalled it. The warning light eventually turned a reassuring green again.

I felt enormously relieved once the problem was solved. Fixing the filter as a team reminded me how much every astronaut depends on one another up here, far from any repair shop on Earth.

Day 3.

Today, I find myself thinking often about home, missing my family deeply and the simple feeling of walking across solid ground. Up here, there is almost no gravity, so our bodies and any loose objects float freely instead of being pulled downward, something most people never notice until they leave it behind, as I have.

I also miss eating fresh food, since every meal on this mission arrives sealed inside small plastic pouches. Even our drinking water is recycled from moisture in the air and from our own sweat, which still feels strange no matter how long I live up here. Meanwhile, the solar panels outside our station quietly collect sunlight. They convert it into the electricity that powers our lights, computers, and life-support systems.

Still, space continues to amaze me every day. Our station orbits Earth so quickly that I can watch the sun rise more than a dozen times within a single day, something I will probably never see so often again after I return home.

Soon, I will return home, but I will never forget this incredible mission among the stars, or the teammates who shared it with me.

versions.title: The Astronaut's Diary
versions.text:
Day 1.

I am an astronaut, and I live aboard a space station that orbits high above Earth, circling the planet roughly once every ninety minutes. Keeping this diary helps me remember each detail of the mission, so I record a new entry every day for students back home.

Up here, everything drifts freely in microgravity, including me, so instead of walking, I pull myself from module to module using handles on the walls. Tools and pens must be tethered to a wall, or they will float off and vanish into some corner of the station.

My daily routine begins with about an hour of exercise, which keeps my muscles and bones strong despite the microgravity. Because the station sees sixteen sunrises a day, our circadian rhythm gets confused, so mission control gives us a strict schedule instead of relying on daylight.

Day 2.

Today, a warning light blinked red, signaling a malfunction in the air filter, the device that removes dust from our air. At first, I felt alarmed, since a malfunctioning filter can endanger the whole crew if it is not fixed quickly.

My crewmate hurried over to help me diagnose the problem. We found that fine dust had clogged the filter's screen over several weeks. We removed it, cleaned every part, and reinstalled it, and the light turned a reassuring green.

I felt enormously relieved once the malfunction was fixed. Repairing it together reminded me how much every astronaut depends on one another, since no repair shop exists for thousands of kilometers.

Day 3.

Today, I find myself thinking often about home, missing my family and the simple feeling of walking on solid ground. Up here, microgravity makes our bodies and any loose object float freely instead of falling down, the way they would on Earth.

I also miss eating truly fresh food, since every meal arrives sealed inside small pouches. Even our water is recycled from humidity in the air and from sweat, and the same life-support system replenishes our oxygen by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen. The solar panels outside the station gather sunlight and turn it into electricity for our lights and computers.

Still, space keeps amazing me. Because the station orbits so fast, nearly eight kilometers each second, I watch the sun rise more than a dozen times in a single day.

Soon, I will go home, but I will never forget this extraordinary mission among the stars.

versions.title: The Astronaut's Diary
versions.text:
Day 1.

I am an astronaut, and I currently live aboard a space station that orbits high above Earth, circling the planet roughly once every ninety minutes. Keeping this diary allows me to preserve every meaningful detail of the mission, so I record a fresh entry each day, partly for myself and partly for students following our progress from home.

Up here, everything drifts freely in microgravity, myself included, so rather than walking through the corridors, I must pull myself from module to module using handles bolted along the walls. Even small tools and pens have to be tethered to a wall or workstation, since otherwise they would float away.

My daily routine always begins with roughly an hour of exercise, which helps preserve muscle and bone strength even though microgravity places almost no strain on either. Because the station experiences sixteen sunrises within a single day, our circadian rhythm becomes thoroughly disrupted, so mission control gives us a strict schedule instead of relying on ordinary daylight.

Day 2.

Today, a warning light suddenly blinked red, signaling a malfunction somewhere within the air filter, the device responsible for removing dust and keeping our air safe to breathe. At first, I felt genuinely alarmed, since an uncorrected malfunction can endanger the whole crew within hours.

My crewmate hurried over from another module to help me diagnose the issue, and together we discovered that fine dust had gradually clogged the filter's screen over several weeks. We removed the unit, cleaned each part by hand, and reinstalled it, and the warning light eventually turned a steady, reassuring green.

I felt enormously relieved once the malfunction had been resolved, since repairing it as a team reminded me how completely every astronaut depends on fellow crew members, especially since no repair shop exists within thousands of kilometers.

Day 3.

Today, I find myself reflecting often on home, missing my family profoundly and the simple, grounded feeling of walking across solid earth. Up here, microgravity causes our bodies and any loose object to float freely rather than being pulled steadily downward, the way they would on Earth.

I also miss eating genuinely fresh food, since every meal arrives sealed inside small plastic pouches rather than served on an open plate. Even our drinking water is recycled from humidity in the cabin air and from our own sweat, and the same life-support system replenishes our oxygen supply by splitting water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. Meanwhile, the solar panels mounted outside our station silently gather sunlight and convert it into the electricity that powers our lights, computers, and life-support systems.

Still, space continues to amaze me every day. Because the station orbits Earth at nearly eight kilometers per second, I get to watch the sun rise more than a dozen times within one ordinary day, a privilege very few people will ever experience firsthand.

Soon, I will return home, but I will never forget this extraordinary mission among the stars.

versions.title: The Astronaut's Diary
versions.text:
Day 1.

I am an astronaut, and I currently reside aboard a space station that orbits our planet at an altitude far above Earth's surface, completing a full circuit approximately once every ninety minutes. Maintaining this diary allows me to retain every meaningful detail of the mission, so I record a fresh entry each day, partly for my own memory and partly for students following our progress from the ground.

Up here, everything drifts freely in microgravity, myself included, so rather than walking through the corridors, I must propel myself from module to module using handles bolted securely along the walls. Even small tools and notebooks must be tethered to a wall or workstation, since otherwise they would drift away unpredictably and vanish into some overlooked corner of the station.

My daily routine invariably begins with approximately an hour of strenuous exercise, which helps retain muscle mass and bone density even though microgravity places almost no mechanical strain on either system. Because the station experiences roughly sixteen sunrises within a single day, our circadian rhythm becomes considerably disrupted, so mission control provides a rigorous schedule rather than relying on ordinary daylight cues.

Day 2.

Today, a warning light unexpectedly blinked red, signaling a malfunction somewhere within the air filter, the device responsible for removing fine dust particles and keeping our air safe to breathe. At first, I felt genuinely alarmed, since an uncorrected filter malfunction can jeopardize the health of the entire crew within hours.

My crewmate hurried over from an adjoining module to help me diagnose the underlying issue, and together we discovered that fine dust had gradually clogged the filter's internal screen over several weeks of continuous operation. We removed the entire unit, cleaned each component by hand, and carefully reinstalled it, and the warning light eventually shifted to a reassuring, steady green.

I felt enormously relieved once the malfunction had been fully resolved, since repairing the filter as a coordinated team reminded me how completely every astronaut depends on fellow crew members, particularly since no repair shop exists within thousands of kilometers of our station.

Day 3.

Today, I find myself reflecting, perhaps more than usual, on home, missing my family profoundly and the simple, grounded sensation of walking across solid, unmoving earth. Up here, microgravity causes our bodies and any loose object to float freely rather than being pulled steadily downward, as they would on Earth.

I also miss eating genuinely fresh food, since every meal arrives sealed inside small plastic pouches rather than served on an open plate at a table. Even our drinking water is recycled meticulously from humidity in the cabin air and from our own sweat, and the same life-support system replenishes our oxygen supply by splitting water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen. Meanwhile, the solar panels mounted outside our station silently gather sunlight and convert it into the electricity that continuously powers our lights, computers, and essential life-support systems.

Still, space continues to amaze me every single day without exception, because the station orbits Earth at nearly eight kilometers per second, letting me watch the sun rise more than a dozen times within one ordinary day, a rare privilege very few people will ever experience firsthand.

Soon, I will return home, but I will never forget this extraordinary mission among the stars, nor the crewmates who became something like a second family to me.

Up here, everything drifts freely in microgravity, myself included. Rather than walking through the corridors, I must propel myself from module to module using handles bolted securely along the walls. Because the station experiences roughly sixteen sunrises within a single day, our circadian rhythm becomes considerably disrupted; consequently, mission control provides a rigorous schedule rather than relying on ordinary daylight cues, which simply do not exist in any dependable sense up here.

Day 2.

Today, a warning light unexpectedly blinked red, signaling a malfunction somewhere within the air filter, the critical device responsible for removing fine dust particles and keeping our air perpetually safe to breathe; at first, I felt genuinely alarmed, since an uncorrected filter malfunction can jeopardize the health of the entire crew within a matter of hours.

My crewmate hurried over from an adjoining module to help me diagnose the underlying issue. Together, we discovered that fine dust had gradually accumulated and clogged the filter's internal screen over the course of several weeks of continuous operation. Methodically, we removed the entire unit, cleaned each component by hand, and carefully reinstalled it piece by piece, and the warning light eventually shifted to a reassuring, steady green.

I felt enormously relieved once the malfunction had been fully resolved. Repairing the filter as a coordinated team reminded me, once again, how completely every astronaut depends on fellow crew members, particularly since no repair shop or spare-parts store exists within thousands of kilometers of our station.

Day 3.

Today, I find myself reflecting, perhaps more than usual, on home, missing my family profoundly and the simple, grounded sensation of walking across solid, unmoving earth. Up here, microgravity causes our bodies and any loose object to float freely rather than being pulled steadily downward, as they would on Earth; on our home planet, gravity holds everything firmly in place, a force so constant that most people rarely notice it until, like me, they leave it behind entirely.

I also miss eating genuinely fresh food, since every meal arrives sealed inside small plastic pouches rather than served on an open plate at a table, and even our drinking water is recycled meticulously from humidity in the cabin air and from our own perspiration. The same life-support system also replenishes our oxygen supply by splitting water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen, systems upon which every crew member depends absolutely. Meanwhile, the solar panels mounted outside our station silently gather sunlight and convert it into the electricity that continuously powers our lights and computers.

Still, space continues to amaze and astonish me every single day without exception, because the station orbits Earth at nearly eight kilometers per second, permitting me to witness the sun rise more than a dozen times within one ordinary day, an extraordinary privilege very few people will ever experience firsthand.

Soon, I will return home, but I will never forget this extraordinary mission among the stars, nor the crewmates who became something like a second family to me during these unforgettable months.

versions.title: The Astronaut's Diary
versions.text:
Day 1.

I am an astronaut, and I currently reside aboard a space station that orbits our planet at an altitude far above Earth's surface, completing a full orbital circuit in approximately ninety minutes, a periodicity that still astonishes me even after months aboard. Maintaining this diary allows me to retain the meaningful details of an experience that would otherwise blur together quickly, so I record a fresh entry daily, partly for my own memory and partly for students following our progress from the ground below.

Up here, everything drifts freely through the cabin in microgravity, myself included, so rather than walking through the corridors as one would on Earth, I must propel myself from module to module using handles bolted securely along the walls. Even small objects such as tools, pens, and notebooks must be deliberately tethered to a wall or workstation, since left unsecured they drift away unpredictably and often vanish into some overlooked corner of the station.

My daily routine invariably begins with about an hour of strenuous, carefully supervised exercise, meant to help preserve muscle mass and bone density, since microgravity places almost no mechanical strain on either system. Because the station experiences roughly sixteen sunrises within a single day, our circadian rhythm becomes considerably disrupted, a disruption that mission control counteracts with a rigorous, externally set schedule rather than the ordinary daylight cues that simply do not exist this far from the ground.

Day 2.

Today, a warning light unexpectedly blinked red, signaling a malfunction somewhere deep within the air filter, the critical device responsible for removing fine dust particles and keeping our air safe to breathe. At first, I felt genuinely alarmed, since an uncorrected filter malfunction can jeopardize an entire crew's health within hours, a possibility none of us ever takes lightly.

My crewmate hurried over from an adjoining module to help diagnose the underlying issue, and together we discovered that fine dust had gradually clogged the filter's internal screen over weeks of continuous, largely unnoticed operation. Methodically, we removed the unit, cleaned each component by hand, and reinstalled it piece by piece, until the warning light finally shifted to a reassuring, steady green that neither of us fully trusted until we rechecked it twice.

I felt enormously, almost disproportionately relieved once the malfunction had been resolved. Repairing the filter as a team reminded me, yet again, how completely every astronaut depends on fellow crew members, particularly given that no repair shop exists within thousands of kilometers of our fragile, orbiting home.

Day 3.

Today, I find myself reflecting, perhaps more than usual, on everything I left behind on Earth, missing my family with an intensity that surprises even me, and especially missing the deceptively simple, grounded sensation of walking across solid, unmoving earth, a sensation I never once appreciated until it vanished from my daily life.

Up here, microgravity causes our bodies and any loose object within reach to float freely rather than being pulled steadily downward, as they invariably would on Earth, where gravity holds every person and object firmly, almost insistently, in place, a force so constant that most people never notice it at all until, like me, they leave it behind.

I also miss eating genuinely fresh food, since every meal arrives sealed inside small plastic pouches rather than served on an open plate at a shared table, and even our drinking water is recycled with remarkable precision from humidity in the cabin air and from our own sweat. The same life-support system also replenishes our oxygen supply by splitting water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen, systems upon which every crew member depends absolutely, while the solar panels mounted outside our station silently gather sunlight and convert it into the electricity that sustains our lights, computers, and life support.

Still, space continues to amaze me every single day, without fail, because the station orbits Earth at nearly eight kilometers per second, letting me witness the sun rise more than a dozen times within one ordinary day, a rare privilege very few people throughout human history will ever experience firsthand.

Soon, I will return home, but I will never forget this extraordinary mission among the stars, nor the crewmates who became, in every meaningful sense, something like a second family during these unforgettable, transformative months.

keyWords.definition: another person who works with you on the same team or mission
keyWords.example: My crewmate helped me carry the heavy box.

keyWords.definition: a part that cleans air or water by catching dirt and dust
keyWords.example: We cleaned the dusty filter in the fan so it could work well again.

questions.stem: What is this diary mostly about?
options: How to build a space station in orbit around Earth with a few workers and a big rocket
An astronaut's days in space, a small problem, and what she misses
How to grow food in space with lamps and with water on a small shelf
A trip to the moon and back with the crew of six and a pilot
questions.why: The diary tells about the astronaut's daily life, the filter problem she fixes, and what she misses about home.

wrong.A: The diary does not explain how to build a station.
wrong.C: The diary does not talk about growing food.
wrong.D: The astronaut is on a space station, not the moon.

questions.stem: What did the astronaut do right after she woke up each morning?
options: She wrote a long letter home
She looked for the lost filter
She did exercise
She floated outside the station
questions.why: On Day 1, she says she wakes up and does exercise before eating breakfast.

wrong.A: She writes her diary, but not right after waking up.
wrong.B: The filter problem happens on Day 2, not every morning.
wrong.D: She never says she floats outside the station.

questions.stem: Why did the warning light on the filter turn red?
options: The filter ran out of power
Dust had blocked it
Her crewmate turned it off
It was too cold
questions.why: The astronaut and her crewmate found that dust had blocked the filter.

wrong.A: The diary says dust was the problem, not power.
wrong.C: Her crewmate helped fix it; she did not turn it off.
wrong.D: The diary never mentions cold causing the problem.

questions.stem: Why do you think the astronaut felt so relieved after Day 2?
options: Because she and her crewmate solved the problem together
Because she found a new filter in a bag that was on the shelf
Because the station landed on Earth that day near the sea
Because the sun stopped rising on the second day
questions.why: She says fixing the filter together made her feel relieved and reminded her how much astronauts depend on teamwork.

wrong.B: She cleaned the old filter; she did not find a new one.
wrong.C: The station stays in space the whole diary.
wrong.D: The sun rising often is a normal part of being in orbit.

questions.stem: Why does the astronaut's food come sealed in bags instead of on an open plate?
options: Bagged food tastes much better in space
Loose food would float away without gravity
There are no plates on the space station
The crew is not allowed to cook
questions.why: Since there is almost no gravity, loose food would float away, so it is kept sealed in bags.

wrong.A: The diary never says the taste is the reason.
wrong.C: The diary does not say plates are missing.
wrong.D: The diary does not mention cooking rules.

questions.stem: How is life on the space station different from life on Earth?
options: On the station there is almost no gravity, but on Earth gravity holds things down
On the station it rains every day, but Earth is dry, said the astronaut
On the station people walk, but on Earth people float in the air
On the station the sun rises once a week, but on Earth it rises once a day
questions.why: The diary explains that on the station things float because there is almost no gravity, while gravity holds things down on Earth.

wrong.B: The diary never mentions rain.
wrong.C: It is the opposite: people float on the station and walk on Earth.
wrong.D: The astronaut sees the sun rise many times a day on the station.

questions.stem: In the diary, the word gravity means —
options: a kind of space food
the pull that holds things down
a tool used to fix filters
a part of the space station in space
questions.why: The diary says gravity is the pull that holds things down on Earth.

wrong.A: Gravity is not a food.
wrong.C: The filter was fixed with cleaning, not with something called gravity.
wrong.D: Gravity is a force, not a station part.

questions.stem: Why did the astronaut most likely write this diary?
options: To complain about her crewmate
To share her mission and feelings with others
To give instructions for building a filter
To describe a trip to a different planet
questions.why: She says she is writing the diary to tell people about her mission, including her daily life and feelings.

wrong.A: She thanks her crewmate for helping her.
wrong.C: The diary is not a how-to guide.
wrong.D: The diary stays on one space station, not a trip to another planet.

LOW.prompt: Would you like to be an astronaut on a space station? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the diary.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the diary.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I would like to be an astronaut. I think it would be amazing to float and to see the sun rise many times a day. I would also like working with a crewmate, because the astronaut and her crewmate fixed the filter together. I know I would miss walking on the ground and eating fresh food, but I still think the mission would be worth it.

keyWords.definition: the curved path something travels around a planet or star
keyWords.example: The small satellite stayed in orbit around Earth for many years.

keyWords.definition: one connected section or room of a spacecraft or space station
keyWords.example: The astronauts moved their experiments into a new module.

keyWords.definition: a set of actions done the same way, again and again
keyWords.example: Brushing your teeth every morning is part of a healthy routine.

keyWords.definition: having to do with the sun, or powered by sunlight
keyWords.example: Our school installed solar panels on the roof.

keyWords.definition: to clean and use something again instead of throwing it away
keyWords.example: We recycle old paper to make new notebooks.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of this diary?
options: An astronaut describes her daily routine, a filter problem she and her crewmate solve, and what she misses about Earth.
An astronaut explains in detail how large rockets are designed, built, and launched into space, and what each part does.
An astronaut frequently complains that the whole space mission was simply not worth all the trouble and the pain.
An astronaut describes an exciting trip to a new planet that has not been visited before, with new friends.
questions.why: The diary covers her routine, the filter malfunction she fixes with her crewmate, and what she misses about home.

wrong.B: The diary does not explain rocket building.
wrong.C: She says space continues to amaze her, so she is not complaining about the mission.
wrong.D: She stays on one orbiting station the whole time.

questions.stem: How many sunrises does the astronaut see each day?
options: Only one each day
Exactly two or three
More than a dozen
One
questions.why: In the story, the station moves so fast that the astronaut sees the sun rise more than a dozen times a day.

wrong.A: The station circles Earth many times a day.
wrong.B: The number is much bigger than two.
wrong.D: The astronaut does see sunrises.

questions.stem: What caused the warning light on the air filter to turn red?
options: A power failure in the module
A mistake the crewmate made while sleeping
Dust that had clogged the filter's screen
Too much sunlight hitting the solar panels
questions.why: The astronaut and her crewmate discovered that fine dust had slowly clogged the filter's screen.

wrong.A: The diary blames dust, not a power failure.
wrong.B: The problem was dust, not a mistake by the crewmate.
wrong.D: The solar panels are not connected to the filter problem.

questions.stem: Why does the astronaut's daily routine include about an hour of exercise?
options: To pass the time because there is nothing else to do all day
To help keep her muscles and bones strong without much gravity
To prepare for a spacewalk later that day outside the station
Because mission control requires it as a punishment for her
questions.why: The diary explains that exercise helps keep her muscles and bones strong since there is almost no gravity pulling on them.

wrong.A: She has clear daily tasks, so exercise is not just to fill time.
wrong.C: The diary never mentions a spacewalk.
wrong.D: Exercise is for her health, not a punishment.

questions.stem: In the diary, the word routine means —
options: a sudden, unexpected problem in the middle of the day
a type of space food that comes in a small bag
a set of actions done the same way each day
a part of the air filter that cleans the cabin
questions.why: Her daily routine is the set of actions, like exercise and breakfast, that she repeats every day.

wrong.A: A routine is planned, not a sudden problem.
wrong.B: Routine is not a kind of food.
wrong.D: The filter and the routine are different things in the diary.

questions.stem: How is the astronaut's drinking water different from drinking water on Earth?
options: It is recycled from moisture in the air and from sweat, instead of coming from rivers or taps
It is brought up fresh from Earth by a cargo ship nearly every single day of the mission
It is made from melted ice that was specially carried up from Earth months ago
It is not needed up here because of the station's complete lack of gravity
questions.why: The diary explains that drinking water on the station is recycled from humidity in the air and from sweat, unlike typical water on Earth.

wrong.B: Bringing fresh water every day would be extremely difficult in space.
wrong.C: The diary does not mention melted ice.
wrong.D: Astronauts still need to drink water despite the lack of gravity.

questions.stem: Why do solar panels matter to life on the space station?
options: They help the filter remove dust from the air inside the station
They allow astronauts to walk normally despite low gravity in space
They are used only to decorate the outside of the station
They collect sunlight and convert it into electricity for the station
questions.why: The diary says the solar panels collect sunlight and convert it into electricity that powers the lights, computers, and life-support systems.

wrong.A: The filter removes dust; the solar panels provide power.
wrong.B: Solar panels do not affect gravity or walking.
wrong.C: The diary describes solar panels as functional, not decorative.

questions.stem: Why does the astronaut most likely describe both the filter problem and what she misses about home?
options: To warn readers never to become astronauts because the work is too hard and unsafe
To give readers a full picture of both the challenges and feelings of life in space
To prove that space stations rarely break down, and that a filter is easy to fix
To explain how to repair machines, from a small filter to a large engine on Earth
questions.why: By sharing both a technical problem and her personal feelings, she helps readers understand the whole experience of living in space.

wrong.A: She still finds space amazing, so she is not warning people away from it.
wrong.C: The filter problem shows that stations can have issues.
wrong.D: The diary describes one specific repair, not general repair instructions.

MID.prompt: Explain how the astronaut and her crewmate solved the filter problem, and why working as a team mattered. Use at least two details from the diary.
checklist: I explained what caused the problem and how it was solved.
I used at least two details from the diary.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The astronaut noticed a warning light blink red on the air filter, which is the part that keeps the air safe to breathe. She and her crewmate investigated together and discovered that dust had clogged the filter's screen. They carefully cleaned it and put it back, and the warning light turned green again. Working as a team mattered because there is no repair shop in space, so astronauts must depend completely on each other to solve problems safely and quickly.

keyWords.definition: a condition with very little gravity, so things float instead of falling
keyWords.example: In microgravity, a dropped pencil will simply hang in the air.

keyWords.definition: a failure of a machine or part to work correctly
keyWords.example: A small malfunction in the robot's wheel made it turn the wrong way.

keyWords.definition: having to do with the body's natural twenty-four-hour clock
keyWords.example: Jet lag happens when travel disrupts your circadian rhythm.

keyWords.definition: a rope, cord, or strap that keeps something from floating or drifting away
keyWords.example: The climber clipped a tether to her harness before stepping onto the ledge.

keyWords.definition: to fill something up again after it has been used
keyWords.example: The hikers stopped at the stream to replenish their water bottles.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of this diary?
options: Life aboard a space station involves a demanding routine, occasional equipment malfunctions, and a deep sense of what is missed from Earth.
Space stations are generally considered far too dangerous for any ordinary astronaut to live aboard safely for long periods while it circles the Earth.
The astronaut secretly regrets having accepted this particular space mission almost immediately after it got underway.
Mission control makes the decisions for the astronauts with little crew input.
questions.why: The diary covers her demanding routine, the filter malfunction, and her reflections on home, giving a full picture of life aboard the station.

wrong.B: She and her crewmate resolve the malfunction safely.
wrong.C: She describes the mission as amazing, not regrettable.
wrong.D: Mission control sets a schedule, but she and her crewmate make the repair themselves.

questions.stem: Why does mission control impose a strict schedule rather than letting astronauts follow natural daylight cues?
options: Because the station was originally designed and built with no windows
Because looking directly at sunlight through the station's windows is considered far too dangerous for the crew
Because sixteen sunrises a day would otherwise disrupt their circadian rhythm
Because astronauts are generally not allowed to make any of their own daily decisions without approval
questions.why: The diary explains that sixteen sunrises confuse the body's circadian rhythm, so mission control provides a fixed schedule instead.

wrong.A: The astronaut describes looking out a window at Earth.
wrong.B: The diary never says sunlight is dangerous to view.
wrong.D: She and her crewmate make their own repair decisions during the malfunction.

questions.stem: Based on the diary, why must tools and pens be tethered to a wall or workstation?
options: Because mission control requires everything to be labeled
Because loose tools could damage the solar panels outside
Because tethered objects charge the station's batteries when they touch it
Because microgravity would otherwise let them drift away and disappear
questions.why: In microgravity, unsecured objects drift away and vanish into corners of the station, so they must be tethered.

wrong.A: The diary does not mention a labeling requirement.
wrong.B: The solar panels are outside the station, not near loose tools.
wrong.C: Tethers secure objects; they do not charge batteries.

questions.stem: In the diary, the word malfunction means —
options: a scheduled daily routine for the whole crew
a failure of a machine or part to work correctly
a kind of food eaten in space by the crew
a tool used to repair solar panels on the ship
questions.why: The malfunction in the air filter is described as a failure that stops it from working correctly.

wrong.A: A routine is planned and repeated; a malfunction is an unexpected failure.
wrong.C: Malfunction does not refer to food.
wrong.D: The malfunction was in the filter, not in a repair tool for solar panels.

questions.stem: How does the life-support system's way of replenishing oxygen compare with simply breathing air on Earth?
options: On the station, oxygen apparently never needs to be replenished or refilled during the entire length of the mission because the crew brings plenty of it from Earth
On the station, oxygen is replenished by splitting water molecules, while on Earth people simply breathe air that is already full of oxygen
On Earth, oxygen is supposedly created by splitting water molecules inside large city water treatment plants
On the station, astronauts grow enough plants to replace their oxygen supply
questions.why: The diary explains that the station's system replenishes oxygen by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen, unlike simply breathing naturally available air on Earth.

wrong.A: The system must actively replenish oxygen because the station is a sealed environment.
wrong.C: This process happens on the station, not in Earth's water plants.
wrong.D: The diary does not mention growing plants for oxygen.

questions.stem: In what order did these events occur in the diary?
options: The filter malfunction is fixed, exercise begins, the warning light turns red at the end
The warning light turns red, the crewmate helps diagnose the issue, the filter is cleaned and reinstalled
The filter is cleaned and reinstalled, the warning light turns red, the crewmate arrives soon afterward
The crewmate arrives, the filter is cleaned, the warning light turns red, and the exercise ends
questions.why: First the warning light blinks red, then the crewmate helps diagnose the problem, and finally the filter is cleaned and reinstalled.

wrong.A: The red light appears before the fix, not after.
wrong.C: The light turns red before the filter is cleaned, not after.
wrong.D: The crewmate arrives after the warning light turns red, not before.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about teamwork in space from the filter malfunction?
options: Mission control fixes problems remotely without crew help, using computers on the ground
Astronauts prefer to solve every problem alone, because teamwork wastes time in space
Astronauts must depend heavily on each other, since no outside repair help is available
Filter problems are too dangerous for the crew to fix, so they wait for rescue
questions.why: Since no repair shop exists within thousands of kilometers, the astronaut and her crewmate must depend on each other to fix problems themselves.

wrong.A: The astronaut and her crewmate make the repair themselves.
wrong.B: Her crewmate hurries over to help, showing she does not work alone.
wrong.D: They successfully diagnose and fix the malfunction together.

questions.stem: Why does the author likely include so many specific details about microgravity, circadian disruption, and recycled water?
options: To discourage anyone from ever wanting to become an astronaut and travel into space
To argue that space stations should be abandoned because they cost too much money
To prove that life in space is identical to life on Earth in every important way
To help readers understand the real scientific challenges of living in space
questions.why: The specific scientific details help readers understand what daily life and its challenges are genuinely like aboard a space station.

wrong.A: She describes space as continually amazing, not discouraging.
wrong.B: The diary shows problems being solved, not abandoned.
wrong.C: The diary emphasizes many ways life in space differs from life on Earth.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says living on a space station for months would be more exciting than hard. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the diary about the astronaut's routine, the malfunction, and what she misses.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the diary.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that living on a space station would be more exciting than hard, even though it is clearly difficult too. The astronaut describes amazing things, like watching the sun rise more than a dozen times a day and floating freely through the modules. The filter malfunction shows that problems do happen, and fixing it required real teamwork since no repair shop exists nearby. Someone might argue that missing her family and fresh food, along with her disrupted circadian rhythm, makes the hardship outweigh the excitement, but she still describes space as continuing to amaze her every single day, which suggests the wonder of the experience matters more to her than its challenges.

LOW.stem: How does the astronaut move around the station?
options: She walks on the floor
She pulls with her hands
She rides in a small car
She jumps off the walls
LOW.why: The diary says she does not walk and pulls herself with her hands.

wrong.A: She says she does not walk up there.
wrong.C: No car is mentioned in the diary.
wrong.D: The diary never says she jumps off walls.

LOW.stem: A warning light blinked on the air filter. What does a filter do?
options: It makes the station spin
It cleans the air
It gives light at night
It holds the crew's food
LOW.why: An air filter cleans the air the crew breathes, so the warning light meant the filter needed fixing.

wrong.A: A filter does not make anything spin.
wrong.C: The light is a warning, not the filter's job.
wrong.D: Food is stored elsewhere.

LOW.stem: Why did the light on the filter turn green?
options: The astronaut went to sleep
The crew turned off the light
Dust was added to the filter
They cleaned the dust away
LOW.why: The crew cleaned the dust that blocked the filter, and then the light turned green.

wrong.A: Sleep did not change the light.
wrong.B: The crew fixed the filter; they did not just turn off the light.
wrong.C: Dust caused the red light, so adding it would not help.

LOW.stem: How does the astronaut feel at the end of the diary?
options: She loves the trip but misses home
She hates the trip and wants to leave
She is bored with space
She is angry at her crewmate
LOW.why: She misses her mom and dad, yet says space is grand and she will not forget the trip.

wrong.B: She calls space grand and says she will remember it.
wrong.C: She still enjoys watching the sun rise many times.
wrong.D: Her crewmate helped her, so she is not angry.

MID.stem: How does the astronaut get from one module to another?
options: She flies with a jet pack
She walks along the floor
She pulls on wall handles
She rides a small cart
MID.why: The diary says she pulls herself from module to module using handles on the walls.

wrong.A: No jet pack is mentioned.
wrong.B: She says she cannot simply walk through the station.
wrong.D: A cart is never mentioned.

MID.stem: In the diary, the word clogged means —
options: blocked up
cleaned well
switched off
broken in half
MID.why: Fine dust built up in the filter and blocked it, which is why the warning light came on.

wrong.B: The crew cleaned the filter after it was clogged.
wrong.C: The filter was blocked, not switched off.
wrong.D: The filter was not broken; it only needed cleaning.

MID.stem: What does the Day 2 entry show about life on the station?
options: Machines never have any problems
Crew members need to help each other
Dust is the only danger in space
Astronauts should work alone
MID.why: The astronaut says fixing the filter as a team showed how much every astronaut depends on one another.

wrong.A: The filter problem shows machines can have trouble.
wrong.C: The diary never says dust is the only danger.
wrong.D: The crewmate's help shows working alone is not the plan.

options: By topic, from smallest to biggest
By place, from Earth to the sun
As a list of rules for astronauts
By day, with new events in each entry
MID.why: The diary has entries for Day 1, Day 2, and Day 3, and each one tells about new events.

wrong.A: The entries are not sorted by size.
wrong.B: The entries follow days, not places.
wrong.C: The diary tells what happened; it gives no rules.

HIGH.stem: How often does the station circle Earth?
options: Roughly once every ninety minutes
About once every day
Close to once every week
Close to once every five minutes
HIGH.why: The diary says the station circles the planet roughly once every ninety minutes.

wrong.B: Once a day is far slower than the diary says.
wrong.C: Once a week is far slower than the diary says.
wrong.D: Every five minutes is much faster than the diary says.

HIGH.stem: What caused the air filter to malfunction?
options: Dust slowly filled its screen over weeks
A crewmate pressed the wrong switch
The solar panels lost their power
Water leaked into the filter
HIGH.why: The crew found that fine dust had clogged the filter's screen over several weeks.

wrong.B: No wrong switch is mentioned.
wrong.C: The solar panels are not tied to the filter problem.
wrong.D: The diary never mentions a leak.

HIGH.stem: In the diary, the word replenishes most nearly means —
options: throws away
fills up again
measures
hides
HIGH.why: The life-support system supplies the oxygen that the crew uses up, so it fills it up again.

wrong.A: The system adds oxygen; it does not throw it away.
wrong.C: Measuring oxygen would not supply more of it.
wrong.D: The system makes oxygen, not hides it.

HIGH.stem: Why does the astronaut mention that no repair shop exists for thousands of kilometers?
options: To say the station is a nice place
To show the crew must fix things alone
To explain why a filter costs a lot
To tell students not to visit
HIGH.why: With no repair shop nearby, the crew has to rely on one another to fix problems.

wrong.A: The sentence is about how far help is, not about being happy.
wrong.C: The diary says nothing about the cost of the filter.
wrong.D: The astronaut writes to share the trip, not to warn students away.
